newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bank stocks outrun stampeding bourse.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bank stocks outrun stampeding bourse.

text.p: Spanish bank stocks, drawing on a major improvement in balance sheets and profits, have outperformed even the bourse's dramatic gains and some analysts say they still have a bit more mileage left.

Banks have outperformed the market for about four years but this trend has sharply accelerated. Since the start of 1997, shares in Spain's top four banks have appreciated far more than the IBEX index of 35 leading shares, which has gained nearly 32 percent.
Shares in leading bank Santander are up 68 percent on the year, while those of close rival Banco Bilbao Vizcaya are up 67 percent. Banco Central Hispano has risen nearly 62 percent.

Even third-largest bank Argentaria has risen 43 percent, although it devoted nearly half its 1996 pre-tax profits to shoring up its balance sheet and is the sole bank among the top four which has not made major acquisitions in Latin America.
"We see them high and expensive but with more potential," said Javier Bernat, analyst at brokerage Inverban.
In June, shares in the top four banks about doubled market gains. On Wednesday two of them continued to pace a market which has just registered an all-time intraday high of 6,855.80.

"I think they are going to keep on rising...more than the bourse. They are rising because of the outlook for profits and the quality of the profits," said Javier Requena, director of analysis at brokerage Benito y Monjardin.
"In the first quarter their profits were above expectations and I think it will be the same at the end of 1997," he said.
On average, analysts see bank earnings rising 20 to 25 percent in 1997, excluding Argentaria.
Among the top four, Requena said, BBV and BCH were the best opportunities. Bernat selects Santander and BBV.
On Tuesday, even Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo praised the Spanish banks clean-up on loans and costs.
The ratio of non-performing loans to total loans has fallen to a level near its historic minimum, having risen to worrying levels in the last recession. Containment of operating costs was continuing.

"These favourable tendencies, which intensified in the first quarter of 1997, have allowed financial institutions to maintain profitability levels both in terms of balance sheets as well as shareholders' funds, that compare satisfactorily with the results of other bankings systems," Rojo said.

Among other good news is growing domestic demand, which should boost consumer loan business. Bond future prices have also risen more than five percent in the second quarter, providing a cushion for own-account trading profits later in the year.
In addition, low interest rates have prompted an exodus of funds from fixed-rate instruments into the bourse, ensuring hefty commission income, Inverban's Bernat added.
Finally, the tantalising prospect of higher growth rates from heavy recent Latin American purchases is adding to the shares' allure.
Still, some people believe there has been too much of a good thing. With such a surfeit of good news, there is hardly anything else positive that could surface.

"They are overvalued...It will be difficult for them (the shares) to rise. They've already discounted an improvement in profitability, rate declines, good markets and a reduction in non-performing loans. There isn't anything left to discount," said an analyst at another Spanish brokerage.
"They are vulnerable to bad news," he added.
On Wednesday, Santander was trading 100 pesetas up at 4,750, while BBV rose 220 pesetas to 11,930 and BCH was 40 pesetas up at 5,440.
